newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian stocks follow Dow lower at quiet open.
newsitem.headline: Australian stocks follow Dow lower at quiet open.

text.p: The Australian share market tracked Friday's Wall Street slide and fell almost across the board at the opening on Monday, gold stocks being the exception.
By 10.15 a.m. (0015 GMT), the All Ordinaries index had fallen 21.1 points to 2,663.1 in modest turnover.
"We're just following the overseas trend. I doubt it'll stay down this much," one Sydney-based institutional dealer said.
Gold shares rose another 1.5 percent on the back of higher bullion prices, after gaining 1.3 percent on Friday.

"It looks as if we're just going to drift a bit lower in light turnover. The gold sector is the only one moving forward at this stage, and it's because of the stronger gold price on Friday," said Steve Mayne of Nevitts in Brisbane.
Among the gold stocks, heavyweight Normandy Mining rose two cents to A$1.59,while Acacia Resources gained 5.1 cents to A$1.43 and St. Barbara Mines seven cents to 40 cents.
Most blue chips lost ground. BHP fell 22 cents to A$18.34, Rio Tinto 30 cents to A$21.50, and WMC seven cents to A$7.80.

Soft drink bottler Coca-Cola Amatil fell 48 cents to A$16.09 after rocketing A$1.53 on Friday when a stronger Philippine peso put the bottler's San Miguel Corp in a positive light. "There is a bit of profit-taking in the stock today," one dealer noted.

Food ingredients group Burns Philp rose eight cents to A$2.50 and Meridian Investment Trust 12 cents to A$1.59 on news of a settlement of the Estate Mortgage legal dispute. Burns Philp will pay Meridian A$90 million in cash and issue it with 12 million convertible notes at A$2.20 each.

The activity in shares of pay TV operator Australis Media remained relatively high as investors awaited news on merger talks with rival operator Foxtel, jointly owned by News Corp and the government's Telstra Corp.
Australis fell 0.5 cents to 21 cents, while News Corp lost 8.8 cents to trade at A$6.17.

Trading in Greenfields Coal was suspended at the stock exchange's request pending clarification of its financial position. Greenfields owns a coal extraction plant in the U.S. and has recently sought funding to help meet the plant's production targets. The stock last traded at 18.5 cents.
